newsitem.title: USA: Political "spin" is a game at Clinton-Dole debate.
newsitem.headline: Political "spin" is a game at Clinton-Dole debate.

text.p: The political "spin" started early and ended late at the first presidential campaign debate of 1996. It almost didn't matter what the candidates said, or how they looked on television.

Hours before Bill Clinton and Bob Dole even began their first debate, their top aides and supporters surged into a makeshift press room in the basement of the Hartford Civic Centre to put their spin on the event.

At the front of the blue-carpeted room was "Spin Alley," complete with a printed sign calling it that, where Clinton and Dole partisans lined up for pre-and-post-debate interviews at 18 separate television positions.

Knots of reporters crowded around the political bigshots, pencils and notebooks poised, straining to hear their "burbling banalities" as White House spokesman Mike McCurry described the barrage of soundbites from the opposing camps.

Republican strategist Jim Cicconi said the debate gave Dole a chance to remind voters "that Clinton has represented himself as something different than he really is." Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said it was a chance for Clinton "to talk about how far this country has come in the last four years."

The verdicts afterwards were swift and predictable. "A big plus for Dole," crowed Republican National Chairman Haley Barbour. "Of course, I'm prejudiced, but I thought the president did very well," former Texas Gov. Anne Richards retorted.

Using "talking points" sharpened by Clinton and Dole speech-writers, goverors, cabinet members, members of Congress and rank-and-file staff buttonholed every reporter they could find, offering pithy quotes.

"It is, on the face of it, ridiculous. You've got hundreds of reporters sitting in a room being cajoled by paid operatives of a campaign who tell you, surprise surprise, that their guy did great." Newsweek writer Matthew Cooper said of the only-in- America instant debate analysis.

"That said," Cooper added, "there's a certain keeping-up- with-the Joneses factor involved. Since your competitors are here, you have to be here." The debate drew 1,300 journalists from throughout the world.
If the outcome of the 90-minute clash between Clinton and Dole was itself a matter of debate among the spin doctors, the Clinton campaign seemed to have a clear organisational advantage.

The Clinton camp issued a "pre-buttal" to what Dole was expected to say before the debate, and five minutes afterwards came out with a five-page, point-by-point rebuttal of Dole's statements in the debate.

It also had orange signs that identified pro-Clinton spinners prowling the pressroom, forcing the Dole camp to improvise with Dole-Kemp campaign posters to tell reporters who was who among the Republicans.

The effort to brainwash the news media has relatively recent origins. It started in 1984 when then-President Ronald Reagan, in his first debate with Democratic challenger Walter Mondale, gave a long, rambling closing statement that caused reporters to wonder if Reagan was showing his age.

To try to quell that political brushfire before it became an inferno, Reagan's top aides boarded the press plane the next morning and, in the now-immortal words of a newsmagazine writer named James Hildrith, gave the debate story a new "spin."

The rest is history, and it's likely to repeat itself on Wednesday in St. Petersburg, Fla. vice-presidential debate between Al Gore and Jack Kemp and again in San Diego, Calif. on Oct. 16 when Clinton and Dole square off again.
